The person, not the role

01 / Who

LinkedIn tells you where I sat. A CV tells you what I was allowed to claim. Neither tells you what it is like to actually work with me, or what I was thinking about while all of that happened. This page tries to.

  • Honest over impressive

    I would rather show a thin end-to-end slice that works than a deep demo that hides what is missing. My studio's domain has a typo on purpose. Imperfect, like life.

  • Standards are a gift, not a gate

    Every team I led got a shared architecture, a review habit and a Gitflow before it got a deadline. People do their best work when the ground is stable under them.

  • Keep the why

    Specs, decisions and their reasons should survive the people who made them. BridgeOS exists because I watched too many projects lose the 'why' between the slide and the code.

  • Teach it to a kid

    If I cannot explain it to a ten-year-old in a Scratch class, I do not understand it yet. Same test for Angular training: if the room is confused, the idea is not finished.

Energised by

  • Turning a vague idea into something runnable in a day
  • Building a team with real chemistry, then getting out of its way
  • Complex data becoming an interface a client understands at a glance
  • Working across Spanish, Czech and English contexts, often in the same week
  • Dogfooding my own tools until they break

Drained by

  • Status theatre and slides that score better than reality
  • Decisions with no owner and no reason attached
  • Rewrites nobody is allowed to finish
  • Meetings that could have been a written decision

Working with Denis · the short manual

Best way to reach me
Email with the actual question in the first line. I answer in kind.
How I give feedback
Direct, specific, about the work, usually in a code review. I assume you want to know.
How I want feedback
The same. Tell me the thing. I will not take it personally.
How I lead
Hire well, set the architecture and the standards early, review everything at the start, then trust. A team of fifteen ran that way for three years.
AI in my workflow
Daily, governed, with a human ratifying anything that ships. Claude Code mostly, local models when budget or data says so.
When I am wrong
I change my mind in public. Ask me what I got wrong last month.

Timeline, in context

02 / 8 acts

Each chapter next to what was going on in the world at the time. Careers make more sense that way.

  1. 2005to 2011

    Economics school, but the computer lab

    Prague University of Economics and Business

    Master's in Information Technology and Systems, minor in Insurance. From 2008 I was already freelancing as a web and graphic designer: e-shops, Drupal builds, print, a career portal for a client in Uruguay. The degree taught me how businesses think. The freelancing taught me how they actually pay.

    Meanwhile

    Prague had joined the EU a year before I started. The iPhone arrived in 2007, the financial crisis in 2008. jQuery was the framework. Nobody called themselves a front-end engineer yet.

  2. 2011to 2012

    First real code, first real users

    Elephant Orchestra · Semantic Visions · Elephant Traffic

    HTML and CSS coder who became a PHP programmer on Zend: the Uspory.cz savings portal and a loan comparator for Slovakia. Then a real-time, highly interactive front-end for IQalerts, which is where JavaScript stopped being decoration and became the product.

    Meanwhile

    Backbone and the first single-page apps. Node.js was new and slightly suspicious. The browser was becoming a runtime and most companies had not noticed.

  3. 2012to 2015

    Cloud ERP, before it was obvious

    ABRA Software, Prague

    Core front-end developer on PrimaERP, a cloud ERP for small teams: time tracking, billing, attendance. Angular 1.x against a Java REST API on AWS, with Grails and Groovy in the mix. I prototyped the next stack in React and Flux before most of Prague had heard of either.

    Meanwhile

    AngularJS won, then React showed up in 2013 and everyone argued. Slack launched. 'Move to the cloud' went from pitch to plan for small businesses.

  4. 2015to 2016

    Founder for the first time

    AlexApp.io, Prague

    Co-founded Alex, a property-management system for small and medium hoteliers. I owned architecture and every technology decision: Angular 1.5 components, Node and Express on PostgreSQL, real-time sync over Socket.IO, i18n from day one. I learned what a product costs when you are the one paying.

    Meanwhile

    Airbnb was eating the small-hotel market from below and Booking.com from above. Every hotelier was a spreadsheet and a phone. The market was right, the timing for a two-person team was hard.

  5. 2016to 2017

    Regulated, at scale

    Casenet (Zyter), Prague, for a US health-insurance platform

    Led development and architecture of a new desktop client for TruCare, serving millions of members. Angular 2 while it was still in release candidates, a Redux-pattern state layer, a custom component set, a real testing strategy. Scrum Master for a five-person US team from six time zones away.

    Meanwhile

    Angular 2 shipped in September 2016 and broke everything Angular 1 knew. US healthcare was mid-ACA and every payer was rebuilding. Remote-first teams were still an oddity.

  6. 2017to 2020

    Fifteen people, twenty-five countries

    NEORIS, Prague, for Cemex GO

    Front-end lead on Cemex GO, the flagship of a global cement company's digital transformation. Built and led a team of up to fifteen on Orders and Schedule, the platform's most complex service, across Monterrey, Prague and Gurgaon. Directed a full rewrite of all client apps while releases kept shipping, set a shared architecture across three apps, introduced Gitflow, ran the technical interviews, helped open the Prague office. The best team I have been part of. Years later I turned the whole genre of 'digital transformation' into a satirical game, because I had lived enough of it to write the exit interview.

    Meanwhile

    Every incumbent was buying a 'Netflix of X' deck. Digital transformation was the phrase of the decade. Prague became a nearshoring hub and distributed teams across three continents became normal.

  7. 2020to 2021

    The pandemic years: an MVP and a life-sciences lead

    Freelance, then EPAM for Abcam, Prague

    Spring 2020: built the MVP of a social platform connecting people through food events and hosting, React 16 with Hooks, Redux, Cypress, in a cross-functional team of five. Launched into the one year nobody could host dinner. Then EPAM: front-end engineer for Abcam, a global life-sciences company, promoted to lead a team of four.

    Meanwhile

    Lockdowns. Remote-everything. Life sciences was suddenly the most important industry on earth, and hospitality the most fragile. A lot of office work turned out to be ritual.

  8. 2021to now

    Fintech interfaces, and AI enters the workflow

    Independent consultant, primarily FinMason (Boston), from Prague

    Long-term engagement with an investment-analytics fintech serving wealth and asset managers. I own UX and front-end together: analytics dashboards, embeddable white-labeled experiences, Angular, React, StencilJS, Remix, Node. In 2023 I brought Claude and LLMs into the delivery process itself, for prototyping, development and code quality, and started thinking hard about how to do that responsibly.

    Meanwhile

    ChatGPT in November 2022 kicked off the LLM wave. By 2024 coding agents could take a spec to a running app, and the question moved from 'can it code' to 'who governs what it builds'.

BridgeOS · 1/4

studio OS · 2025 to now

BridgeOS

AI-native product-spec workspace that builds the app from approved specs and keeps watching it in production. Event-sourced ledger, executable specs, human ratification gates. Spanish-first, local-first, built by dogfooding itself.

The idea

Problem

A build agent cannot reliably turn prose specs into a working app. Every ambiguity in the spec becomes a silent decision the agent makes for you, and nobody remembers why.

Bet

Each ambiguity gets its own structured contract the build must honour. Specs move through phases (idea, business, product, UX, architecture, security, infra, development, testing), a human ratifies each gate, and an event-sourced ledger keeps the why forever.

The stack

Next.jsTypeScriptGoSQLiteDockerClaude CodeLM Studio (local models)Spanish-first UI

How it is built

Local-first: runs against LM Studio with no paid keys. Built by dogfooding itself: BridgeOS builds the apps in this list.

AI film harness and studio · 1/4

AI film · 2026, full-time

AI film harness and studio

Resumable pipeline from idea to assembled short film, with a review studio: cast, shot grid, per-shot regenerate, provider swap, timeline.

The idea

Problem

Video models can make a beautiful shot. They cannot make forty shots of the same person in the same story. The bottleneck is not the model, it is consistency, taste and pipeline discipline.

Bet

A resumable pipeline from idea to cut, with a review surface at every stage so a human approves before anything expensive runs. Provider-agnostic: swap models per shot.

The stack

Python harnessNext.js studioPer-stage approvalCharacter sheetsKeyframes and video rendersLip sync and QCProvider catalog and key vault

How it is built

The harness runs the pipeline and resumes from any stage. The studio shows the project board, cast, shot grid with per-shot regenerate, timeline scrubber and live run log.

Character Consistency Test · 1/4

experiment · 2026

Character Consistency Test

The one experiment that decides whether an AI movie studio is buildable. Runs for under 30 euro, mostly on local hardware.

The idea

Problem

Does one character's identity survive across roughly forty varied shots, different angles, lighting, shot sizes and wardrobe, well enough that an audience reads it as one person?

Bet

If yes, an AI movie studio is an engineering problem. If no, nothing downstream matters. So run this first, for under thirty euro, before building anything else.

The stack

Local image generationIdentity referencesScored shot matrixOne paid animation stage, 3 to 4 shots

How it is built

Stages one to three run on my own hardware. Only the animation stage touches a paid API.
